title: Disk-streamed 80B inference misses 4.5 tokens a second when retested by H2 2027
body: Swiftlet, a Swift and Metal runtime published on August 4, reports Qwen3-Next-80B — 42 gigabytes of weights on disk — generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac while peaking at 4.3 gigabytes of resident memory, by holding the dense layers permanently loaded at four bits and streaming the routed experts off storage into a cache the user sizes with a command-line flag. The mechanism is real and the arithmetic hangs together: the model fires only about three billion parameters per token, so what has to move per token is a fraction of the file rather than the file. What the claim does not carry is the set of conditions that make a throughput number mean anything once weights stream instead of sitting resident. No context length is given, no batch size, no split between prompt processing and decoding, and the quantization is stated only for the dense part. Those conditions stop being bookkeeping here and become the measurement itself. The author's own figures show the expert cache hitting between 43 and 70 percent depending on how much memory it is handed, and throughput barely moving across that range, because the bottleneck currently sits in GPU dispatch rather than in reading from storage. So the rate is set by how much dispatch a run demands, and the condition that decides that is the one the author never varied and never stated: a longer prompt touches more distinct experts across a generation, and every figure here was taken at a context length nobody outside can name. That is exactly what a single number cannot express. Today's other local-inference item has the same shape: Unsloth's Studio merge adds image and video generation on the project's own GGUF quantizations with a batching speedup the team measured itself, and no package release to test it against. The prediction is that the headline figure here is a warm-cache, short-context best case and will not survive being measured by anyone else. By the end of H2 2027, a measurement published by someone other than the runtime's author — running an 80-billion-class sparse mixture-of-experts model under expert streaming on Apple silicon — reports a decoding rate below 4.5 tokens a second, stated together with the context length it was measured at. There are two ways this is wrong. If such a measurement appears under those stated conditions and lands at 4.5 tokens a second or above, the call fails on substance. If no measurement stating those conditions appears at all by the end of 2027, it fails on silence, and the number stays what it is today: one figure, from the party that produced it, describing a run whose conditions nobody outside can name.

reasoning.because: Swiftlet reports 4.5 to 5 tokens a second for an 80B model at 4.3 GB resident, no context stated
reasoning.given: Dispatch bounds the rate, not the cache budget the author swept, so context length is the condition never varied or stated
reasoning.so_that: An outside measurement states the context length and reports under 4.5 tokens a second
reasoning.landing: by H2 2027; a third-party measurement with the context length stated
reasoning.plain_language: A new app says a huge AI model runs fast on a Mac. When outsiders test it properly, expect a smaller number.

summary: Swiftlet reports an 80-billion-parameter Qwen generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac in 4.3 gigabytes of memory by streaming its experts off disk, with no context length or batch size stated. Expect an outside measurement, conditions stated, to come in under 4.5 by H2 2027.
